meta.titre: Radioactive Decay: Nuclear Equations, Decay Series and Half-Life Calculations

sections.contenu_markdown: In the hospitals of Yaounde and Douala, a doctor may use a radioactive tracer to scan a patient, and in laboratories across the world archaeologists use the same kind of physics to say how old a piece of charcoal from an ancient village fire pit really is. Both uses rely on one fact: unstable nuclei change by themselves, at a rate that nothing a chemist does in a flask can alter. The GCE examiners ask you to balance nuclear equations, to count the particles emitted in a decay series and to work with half-lives, because these tasks test careful bookkeeping of numbers rather than memorised facts.

items: An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons, and the number of protons defines the element.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
A beam of charged particles is deflected by an electric field towards the plate of opposite charge.

sections.contenu_markdown:
**Nuclide notation.** A nuclide is written ${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}$, where $A$ is the nucleon number (protons plus neutrons) and $Z$ is the proton number. The number of neutrons is $A - Z$.

**Radioactive decay** is the spontaneous, random breakdown of an unstable nucleus. It is not affected by temperature, pressure or whether the atom is in a compound, because chemical changes involve only the outer electrons while decay is a change inside the nucleus.

| Radiation | Symbol | Change in nucleus | Charge | Relative penetration | Ionising power |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha, $\alpha$ | ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$ | $A$ falls by 4, $Z$ falls by 2 | $+2$ | Stopped by paper or a few cm of air | Strongest |
| Beta-minus, $\beta^-$ | ${}^{\ 0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$ | $A$ unchanged, $Z$ rises by 1 (a neutron becomes a proton) | $-1$ | Stopped by a few mm of aluminium | Medium |
| Gamma, $\gamma$ | high-energy photon | No change in $A$ or $Z$ | $0$ | Reduced, never fully stopped, by thick lead | Weakest |

In an electric field $\alpha$ particles are deflected towards the negative plate, $\beta^-$ particles towards the positive plate (much more strongly, as they are far lighter), and $\gamma$ rays are not deflected.

**Balancing a nuclear equation.** The total nucleon number $A$ and the total charge (proton number $Z$) must be equal on both sides. For example, ${}^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} \rightarrow {}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$ balances because $226 = 222 + 4$ and $88 = 86 + 2$.

**Half-life.** The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay, equivalently the time for the activity to fall to half. It is constant for a given nuclide, so decay is a first-order process. After $t$ the number of undecayed nuclei is
$$N = N_0\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/t_{1/2}}$$
and the decay constant is $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$. The rate of decay (the activity) is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei, $\text{activity} = \lambda N$.

variantes.nom: Counting the particles in a decay series
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question gives the starting and final nuclides and asks how many alpha and beta particles were emitted.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Only $\alpha$ emission changes the nucleon number, so the number of alpha particles is $a = \dfrac{A_{\text{start}} - A_{\text{end}}}{4}$. Each alpha lowers $Z$ by 2 and each $\beta^-$ raises it by 1, so $Z_{\text{end}} = Z_{\text{start}} - 2a + b$ and $b = Z_{\text{end}} - Z_{\text{start}} + 2a$. For ${}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U} \rightarrow {}^{206}_{82}\mathrm{Pb}$: $a = \dfrac{238 - 206}{4} = 8$ and $b = 82 - 92 + 16 = 6$. A negative value of $b$, or a value of $a$ that is not a whole number, shows that the question involves a different decay mode or that you have made an error.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked for the mass, number of nuclei or activity remaining after a given time, or the time taken to fall to a given fraction.
variantes.contenu_markdown: After 1, 2, 3, 4 half-lives the fraction remaining is $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{4}$, $\frac{1}{8}$, $\frac{1}{16}$. For times that are not whole numbers of half-lives, use $N = N_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/t_{1/2}}$ directly. To find a time from a fraction $f = N/N_0$, take logarithms: $t = t_{1/2}\,\dfrac{\ln(1/f)}{\ln 2}$. Keep the time and the half-life in the same unit, and convert to seconds only when $\lambda$ is needed in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why a particular isotope is chosen for dating, medical tracing or industrial thickness gauging.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Carbon-14 dating uses the fact that living material takes in carbon-14 from the atmosphere and that its activity per gram halves every 5730 years after death. A medical tracer should emit gamma rays (they leave the body) and have a short half-life (so little radiation remains afterwards). A source used to treat deep cancer tumours is a strong gamma emitter. For safety, keep sources shielded (lead for gamma), keep your distance, and limit exposure time.

sections.enonce_markdown: Thorium-232, ${}^{232}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$, is the first member of a natural radioactive series that ends with the stable nuclide ${}^{208}_{82}\mathrm{Pb}$. Only alpha and beta-minus emissions are involved. (a) Calculate how many alpha particles and how many beta-minus particles are emitted in the whole series. (b) A sample of another radioisotope, Q, has a half-life of $6.0$ hours and an initial mass of $80.0\ \mathrm{mg}$. Calculate the mass of Q left after $15.0$ hours, and the decay constant of Q in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

etapes.action: Find the number of alpha particles from the fall in nucleon number.
etapes.justification: Only $\alpha$ emission changes $A$, and each $\alpha$ removes 4 units.

etapes.action: Find the number of beta particles from the charge balance.
etapes.justification: Six alphas lower $Z$ by 12, so $90 - 12 = 78$, but the final nuclide has $Z = 82$. Each $\beta^-$ raises $Z$ by 1.

etapes.action: Check by writing the full equation.
etapes.justification: The sum of $A$ and the sum of $Z$ must be equal on both sides.

etapes.action: Find the number of half-lives and the mass remaining.
etapes.justification: The number of half-lives is time divided by half-life; the mass is multiplied by one half each time.
Convert the half-life to seconds first, then use $\lambda = \ln 2 / t_{1/2}$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The series emits **6 alpha and 4 beta-minus particles**; after 15.0 hours **14.1 mg** of Q remains and its decay constant is **$3.21\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$**.

items.erreur_markdown: “Beta-minus emission lowers the mass number by 1, because an electron is lost.”
items.pourquoi_faux: The emitted electron comes from a neutron turning into a proton, and an electron has negligible mass compared with a nucleon. The nucleon number is therefore unchanged and the proton number rises by 1.
items.correction_markdown: For $\beta^-$ decay: $A$ stays the same and $Z$ increases by 1. For example ${}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{\ 0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$.

items.erreur_markdown: “After two half-lives the whole sample has decayed.”
items.pourquoi_faux: In each half-life half of the remaining nuclei decay, not half of the original number. After one half-life $50\%$ remains and after two half-lives $25\%$ remains.
items.correction_markdown: Multiply by $\frac12$ once per half-life: after two half-lives the fraction left is $\left(\tfrac12\right)^2 = \tfrac14$.

items.erreur_markdown: “Heating the sample makes the half-life shorter.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Radioactive decay is a nuclear process. Temperature, pressure and chemical combination change collisions between electrons but leave the nucleus unaffected.
items.correction_markdown: The half-life of a nuclide is a constant of that nuclide; only a change of nuclide changes it.

items.erreur_markdown: “An alpha particle lowers the proton number by 4.”
items.pourquoi_faux: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$: it carries away 4 nucleons, of which 2 are protons. So $A$ falls by 4 but $Z$ falls by only 2.
items.correction_markdown: Write the particle in full as ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$ and subtract both numbers: ${}^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra}$ becomes ${}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn}$.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Radium-226, ${}^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra}$, decays by alpha emission. Write the nuclear equation, identify the daughter nuclide and state its number of neutrons. (b) Carbon-14, ${}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}$, decays by beta-minus emission. Write the nuclear equation.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Subtract ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$: $A = 226 - 4 = 222$ and $Z = 88 - 2 = 86$, and element 86 is radon.

${}^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} \rightarrow {}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$

The daughter has $222 - 86 =$ **136 neutrons** (radium-226 had $226 - 88 = 138$).

(b) The nucleon number stays at 14 and $Z$ rises by 1, so the daughter has $Z = 7$ (nitrogen).

**${}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{\ 0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$**

Check: $A$: $14 = 14 + 0$; $Z$: $6 = 7 + (-1)$.

items.enonce_markdown: A radioisotope X has a half-life of $5.0$ years. A freshly prepared source has an activity of $1200$ counts per second. Calculate (a) its activity after $15.0$ years, (b) the time taken for the activity to fall to $37.5$ counts per second, and (c) its activity after $12.5$ years.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $15.0 / 5.0 = 3$ half-lives, so the activity is multiplied by $\left(\tfrac12\right)^3 = \tfrac18$: $1200 / 8 =$ **150 counts per second**.

(b) Halving repeatedly: $1200 \rightarrow 600 \rightarrow 300 \rightarrow 150 \rightarrow 75 \rightarrow 37.5$. That is 5 half-lives, so $t = 5 \times 5.0 =$ **25 years**.

(c) $12.5 / 5.0 = 2.5$ half-lives, so activity $= 1200 \times \left(\tfrac12\right)^{2.5} = 1200 \times 0.1768 =$ **212 counts per second** (3 s.f.).

items.enonce_markdown: Living wood has a constant carbon-14 activity per gram of carbon. The half-life of carbon-14 is $5730$ years. (a) Calculate the decay constant of carbon-14 in $\mathrm{year^{-1}}$. (b) A wooden bowl from an excavation has an activity per gram of carbon equal to $60.0\%$ of that of living wood. Calculate its age. (c) A different sample has an activity per gram equal to $\frac{1}{1024}$ of the living value. Calculate its age and comment on why carbon-14 dating becomes unreliable for samples much older than this.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{5730} =$ **$1.21\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{year^{-1}}$**.

(b) The fraction remaining is $0.600$, so
$t = t_{1/2}\,\dfrac{\ln(1/0.600)}{\ln 2} = 5730 \times \dfrac{0.511}{0.693} = 5730 \times 0.737 \approx$ **$4.22\times10^{3}$ years**.

(c) $1024 = 2^{10}$, so 10 half-lives have passed: $t = 10 \times 5730 =$ **57 300 years**.

After about ten half-lives the activity is only about $0.1\%$ of the starting value, which is comparable to the background count rate and to the effect of tiny contamination by modern carbon. The measurement then has too large an uncertainty to give a reliable age.

items_markdown: Write nuclides as ${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}$. In a nuclear equation the sums of $A$ and of $Z$ are equal on both sides.
$\alpha$ emission: $A$ falls by 4 and $Z$ by 2. $\beta^-$ emission: $A$ unchanged, $Z$ rises by 1. $\gamma$ emission: no change in $A$ or $Z$.
Number of alphas $= \Delta A / 4$; then number of betas $= Z_{\text{end}} - Z_{\text{start}} + 2a$.
Half-life is constant for a nuclide and is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state; $N = N_0(\frac12)^{t/t_{1/2}}$ and $\lambda = \ln 2 / t_{1/2}$.
Alpha is the most ionising and least penetrating; gamma is the least ionising and most penetrating; beta is in between, and alpha and beta are deflected in opposite directions in an electric field.
